scope: One additional stomatopod for the species guide, illustrative reef encounters and optional identification/recall activities. The model depicts one green, gold and red adult appearance without assigning sex or reproductive state. New copy is paraphrased from primary taxonomic/experimental research and museum, university and aquarium accounts.
iucnYearConvention: Use NE and null assessment/publication dates. SeaLifeBase's current indexed IUCN 2025-2 export explicitly reports Not Evaluated, corroborated by Georgia Aquarium and Tennessee Aquarium. No actual global assessment or assessment year was located. General aquarium statements that the animal is not threatened are not treated as an IUCN Least Concern assessment. NE is not evidence that populations are secure.

specimens.name: Peacock mantis shrimp
marks: Large stalked compound eyes sit high above the head
Club-bearing striking limbs fold beneath the front of the body
Pale-edged dark spots mark the front sides of the carapace
The segmented abdomen ends in a broad fan of telson and paired uropods
specimens.role: Predator of hard-shelled invertebrates in reef food webs.
specimens.fact: A strike can create cavitation bubbles; their collapse adds another brief force pulse after the club’s impact.
specimens.habitat: Indo-West Pacific coral and rocky reefs, with shelters among rubble or adjoining sand and gravel. It often occupies burrows near the base of reefs.
specimens.diet: Crabs, snails and other mollusks. Club-like striking limbs help it break hard shells rather than grasp prey with ordinary pincers.
specimens.behavior: Often shelters in a burrow and emerges to forage. Its eyes can move independently while the striking limbs remain folded beneath the body between strikes.
specimens.observe: Compare its folded clubs, prominent stalked eyes and broad tail fan with the harlequin shrimp’s flattened paddle-like claws. Look for pale-edged spots on the carapace sides. Green, red and gold are one appearance; body colour varies, so use several structures together.

claimSupport.acceptedName: Current WoRMS accepts Odontodactylus scyllarus (Linnaeus, 1758), AphiaID 220297, in Stomatopoda. The 2025 primary treatment independently uses this name. Cancer scyllarus is the original combination; the illustrated animal is not a decapod shrimp despite the common name.
claimSupport.marks: Australian Museum's Lizard Island account identifies lateral leopard-like carapace spots and a smashing club. Ahyong's primary taxonomic descriptions support pale-edged spots, rounded compound eyes, segmented abdomen, telson and paired uropods. The 2009 primary eye study's Fig. 1 shows the large independent eyes and folded striking limbs. None of these broad learning marks is claimed to diagnose every wild specimen alone.
claimSupport.roleDiet: Georgia Aquarium documents a diet of crustaceans and mollusks. National Aquarium corroborates crabs and gastropods. Patek and Caldwell's experiments establish shell-breaking impact/cavitation mechanics; these experimental prey observations are not treated as a complete wild diet inventory.
claimSupport.fact: Patek and Caldwell (2005) measured direct limb-impact and subsequent bubble-collapse force peaks. The guide makes a qualitative statement only, without universal force/speed numbers, a guaranteed bubble on every strike or a claim of the fastest punch among all animals.
claimSupport.habitatBehavior: Ahyong's Taiwan account describes reef-flat to reef-base shelters beneath coral and boulders. Lizard Island records rubble-constructed burrows at 10–20 m. University of Texas DigiMorph describes U-shaped gravel burrows. Georgia Aquarium supports emergence to forage; the eye study supports independent eye movement and resting folded appendages.
claimSupport.colourStageSex: Primary life-colour accounts describe reddish-brown through green bodies, pale-edged dark carapace spots, orange-yellow antennal scales, red limb/segment accents and blue uropods with red marginal setae. Large males may be deep green, but the model does not assign reproductive anatomy or offer a colour-only sex key. One adult palette is illustrated rather than a juvenile sequence or fixed geographic colour morph.
claimSupport.sizeDepth: Nominal 14 cm refers to approximate body length, not antenna-tip span. Primary revisions record individuals around this scale and report a specimen length of 171 mm; aquarium/museum summaries round the upper size to 18 cm. The 2025 primary species treatment explicitly reports 0–100 m, matching current SeaLifeBase. Ahyong's older account says to 30 m; Georgia Aquarium gives to 40 m; Lizard Island's 10–20 m is local observation, not a global range. No 100 m individual was independently verified here.
claimSupport.iucn: SeaLifeBase explicitly labels Not Evaluated in its current indexed IUCN Version 2025-2 (Global) export. Georgia Aquarium also states NE. No category or assessment date is inferred from availability in the aquarium trade or from generic population-security statements.
claimSupport.comparison: The one-way harlequin_shrimp link compares two colourful crustacean body plans: folded striking clubs and a broad stomatopod tail fan versus the existing harlequin shrimp's flattened paddle-like claws. It does not assert that the two are close relatives or the nearest species-level lookalikes. Preserve the existing record exactly.

specimens.caution: The simplified model is a learning aid, not a definitive wild species or sex key. Fine ocular scales, tail ridges and claw teeth used in taxonomic diagnoses may be simplified. Do not locate the characteristic leopard pattern on the clubs instead of the carapace sides. Avoid boxy hammerhead eyes, a fish-like tail, oversized ordinary pincers or a decapod walking-leg layout. Colour varies with individuals, size and sex. No claim that this animal sees more colours than humans, detects infrared, has a fixed number of perceptual colour dimensions or experiences the tool's vivid view is made. No lifelong-pairing, universal aggression, population-security or aquarium-care claim is imported.

modelProvenance.nominalDimension: Approximate body length along the head-to-telson axis, excluding antenna and fringe extent
modelProvenance.representative: One illustrative green/green-brown adult with gold/orange antennal scales, pale-edged dark carapace spots, red limb/segment accents and blue tail paddles. Colour sources note sex and size variation, including deep green large males. The simplified model assigns no sex or reproductive anatomy and is not a colour-only sex key.
modelProvenance.basis: Nominal 14 cm body length lies within the measured adult scale in primary revisions. Their reported 171 mm specimen and the museum/aquarium rounded maximum of 18 cm are not claimed as identical exact limits. Depth follows the explicit 0–100 m species interval in the primary 2025 treatment and current SeaLifeBase; older primary shelter accounts to 30 m, aquarium accounts to 40 m and local Lizard Island observations at 10–20 m remain disclosed. The model represents a shallow reef encounter, not equal habitat suitability throughout that interval.
modelProvenance.anatomy: Broad rounded/oval compound corneas on separate stalks with a restrained mid-band; antennules distinct from plate-like antennal scales; small triangular rostral plate; a carapace with pale-edged lateral dark spotting; folded stout raptorial appendages with a rounded striking heel; smaller feeding appendages; three posterior walking-leg pairs; six abdominal somites with subtle pleopods beneath; a distinct ridged telson between paired uropods, each bearing an inner and outer paddle. Blue tail paddles carry restrained red marginal setae.
modelProvenance.anatomyLimits: Do not use rectangular eye bars, exaggerated human-like pupils, oversized ordinary lobster pincers, four or five posterior walking pairs, a single fish tail, or leopard spots displaced onto the clubs. Fine mouthparts, claw teeth, ocular scales and tail ridge counts may be simplified and are not a wild species key. No eggs, gonopores or other sex-specific structures. Pigmentation and modest material highlights do not represent fluorescence, bioluminescence or the animal's spectral perception.
modelProvenance.motion: Conservative bottom pose near rubble, with planted posterior walking legs, slow independent eye/stalk movements and subtle antennular motion. Resting clubs remain folded rather than striking continuously. This illustrative pose does not claim the animal never walks, swims, hunts or leaves its burrow. No new locomotion or combat/cavitation simulation is required.
